abstract: Intratumoral heterogeneity is hypothesized to be a major contributor to treatment resistance, yet the processes that generate it remain only partially understood. New technologies enable measurement of gene expression in individual tumor cells while also determining where the cells are located within a tumor and how they are related through cell division. A central question for such data is how much gene expression differences reflect characteristics passed from parent cells to their descendants, rather than influences from their local surroundings. Distinguishing these influences is challenging because closely related cells often reside near one another. Existing methods examine the relationship between gene expression and each of these factors separately, and can therefore incorrectly attribute spatial effects to ancestry or inherited effects to spatial location. Here, we present SOUR, a statistical method that uses both cell ancestry and spatial location to estimate their respective contributions to differences in gene expression. Using simulated data and two spatial lineage tracing datasets, we demonstrate that SOUR can estimate the separate contributions of cell ancestry and spatial location to variation in gene expression, while substantially reducing the confounding observed with existing approaches.
